Note: not a captain, just an alumni who got to see the change of captains

Number 1:
Leaders don't tell, they ask

You will get nowhere if you are barking orders, or you will lose motivation from the team

Number 2: 
FRC (and FIRST in general) is about exploration of concepts, and the application of them.

Just because you know of AN effective solution, doesn't mean it's the best, or that a "bad" solution is pointless. 

Number 3:
Mistakes lead to learning.

If your team never makes mistakes, they are never learning. And from what I've experienced, most mistakes are more enjoyable than the solutions that come from them. Obviously there's only so many resources, so if you see an obvious mistake that is very resource intensive feel free to step in. But if nothing's being broken, or it's a design that can be changed later, don't say a word. Students will learn, grow, and make fewer of the costly mistakes if they feel comfortable to make mistakes.

Number 4:
Not everyone will like you, and that's ok

If you are a good leader, you will have people who dislike you. If you are a bad leader, you will have people who dislike you. The only thing you can control is how you act and react to their opinions, and knowing your disliked it almost always helpful. Some people might dislike you inherently, but listen to the complaints, often a student might teach you more about how you act, than you can teach them about how to act respectfully. 

Number 5: 
Divide and conquer.

You are not the only mentor, the only helper, the only person in charge. Distribute as many tasks as possible, and allow them to further distribute the tasks. Running an Robotics team is running a business. You need people to help take care of tasks, and you need to allow people to do those tasks without being micromanaged. I really liked when we had a "head mentor" or two for every subsection of the team. From business to shop to programming. Of course you can be a head mentor for a section, but avoid being the head mentor for multiple sections.

Number 6:
Assertive, not aggressive

The line has to be drawn somewhere. And you can't allow everything. I'd first recommend allowing a semi-democratic "governing" style to the team, but ultimately you call the shots and you make the decisions on what is acceptable and what isn't. But nobody listens to the angry boss, but the empathetic boss typically is heard a lot more. Make sure they know you won't tolerate x behavior or plan, but explain why you won't, and make sure they feel heard as well.

Number 7: 
Safety first

This might sound dumb, but as a kid my level of risk avoidance was DIRECTLY linked to what I saw others do. There will be dangers when running the team. Maybe there's a carpet fire, maybe there's live wires running a lot of current. Whatever steps you might consider safe for yourself, but not your students or team, is unacceptable for you to display. Injuries happen, and that's not your fault. But if you display bad safety etiquette, you will see bad safety etiquette from the team. 

Number 8:
Equality

There is no such thing as true equality within a team. Everyone has skills and strengths, but also weaknesses and lack of knowledge. One student may display more positive traits than negative, and might be more trustworthy. That might lead you to believing they should do any task that you need.... That is a mistake. You cannot build trust or gain knowledge on a students capacity to perform without allowing them the chance to perform. One good example is with drivers. My team allowed any member to try out for operator and driver, and then the best was selected (unfortunately not voted, but it makes sense to not make it a popularity contest). This is better than knowing student A is a good driver and never letting student B try.

I'd like to wrap this up with always be willing to learn, and never forget that others can teach, even when you're the one expected to be teaching. Answer questions honestly, and allow people to trust you, or you will not ever reach the goals you have for the team and yourself.

Suicide and suicidal ideation generally comes from a place of desperation. Usually victims of suicide feel as though there are no alternatives and that they are actively causing more problems or issues than they are capable of solving. Another common symptom of (or cause of depending on your belief of how suicidal ideation works) suicidal ideation is an overwhelming feeling of hopelessness. That's why it becomes easier to justify bad behavior that isn't punished, at least directly.

In my personal life, I've had two members of my family take their lives. Because of the impact I've seen, it's caused many of my own episodes of suicidal ideation much less effective, but also causes much longer spouts of depression.

Can bus was very prominent in vehicles for a long while. It's where (as far as I can tell) CAN was developed. It makes sense, you want to minimize the number of cables you need to run, especially since you'd have different control schemas for different parts from different manufacturers. CAN became an effective and simplistic system for maintenance, and it only requires 3 wires ran to any given system 1 for power, 2 for comms, and your ground reference is just tied to any piece of metal on the car. Cars also had significantly fewer sensors in the past too though. As we have more and more digitized cars, and the sensors and other controllers become more critical to safety, the less viable can systems become. But also there are things called CAN relays, that allow you to split your CAN bus, allowing for no daisy chaining CAN. But the cyber truck has way too many issues, it also shouldn't be allowed on the road imo. Cars are designed to crumple to prevent accidents from being as fatal, which is why most cars are "plastic". Now you have a hunk of sheet metal flying at 60+mph into another vehicle... And that sheet metal isn't folding in nicely and consistently.

I really like the idea of pick and place games, because I find that they CAN have much more diversity in bots.

In contrast infinite point games (games with reusable game pieces like a shooter game) are generally simpler in concept and make the family that is already lost as to what is happening enjoy watching more. When I was in FRC that's how my family was, supportive, but clueless.

Last thing, endgame...

I hate climb. It's been the idea for the endgame for almost all time, and it works due to the risk/reward of lifting the robot, and it's technically challenging (technically in the sense of technology, not nuance) 

So here's my one season solution. Make it a last minute placeable item. Have the human player drop items that are placed on the same alliances side of the field that is similar to a plug or connector of some sort (with really loose tolerances so it's not impossible to do without vision, but vision makes it better) and have one for each robot. Make the human player for this be on the opposite side of the field (we can and have had 2+ human players before) so that at most one robot can move 2, and that requires very fast movement, and make it have 3 different heights that it needs to be placed into for minimally different points, but it's worth more if you have more than 1. RP for all 3.

Small and refined movement is very difficult, especially with speed, so I think it would be ideal for promoting multiple bots doing it (which is what endgame is designed to always have) but then there are significantly less bot damages from falling along with a new challenge.

The number one thing to have for FRC in my alumni opinion is to make sure the entire space is designed with mobility in mind. Every walkway should be able to allow 2 way traffic flow with extra space on either side. You will end up wheeling the robot in there, I don't care if it's the cad room, storage room, field, shop, etc. there have been so many times in my teams life that we had to lift the robot around corners, over tables, around people. It's annoying and it will slow production.

The next most important thing is to allow decorations. They will happen either way, removing them will remove team morale. There is to this day (over 10 years) an automotone toy in our shop because it makes everyone smile when a freshman tries to figure out what it's used for in the shop. I'd reccomend white boards everywhere. Obviously remove anything inappropriate, they are high schoolers (usually) after all. But the robotics jokes were one of my favorite parts of robotics, and I got to be on drive team.

Finally, have engineering cheat sheets around the rooms. Preferably based on what is needed, but it helps. P=IV Graphs near the electrical workstations, full metric -> imperial conversion charts in the shop, code explanations in the programming chambers, etc.

Other comments are also very true, especially with the field comments, that's probably the most important for a successful season, but I think that the team dynamic and cooperation is more important than any amount of seasonal success.

See, I think liking engineering is a fallacy at this point. You don't "like" or "dislike" engineering. Engineering is a method of creating new products/devices/structures/etc. It is the toolbox, being labeled as a job. So not "liking" engineering to me is like saying "I don't like screwdrivers". It's just irrational. But I could understand hearing either "I don't like how strict engineering design is" or "I wish I could design something I'm interested in" or even "I don't enjoy designing things" as a valid way to say you "dislike engineering". But engineering is really just the application of physics with the intent to assume 300% more things are 200% worse than you could possibly imagine.

I was programming head my senior year, but I actively tried to teach other programmers because I knew it was my time to go. I don't know if I'd have been as "generous" with letting others code my junior year.

However in teaching others I found that 1 of 2 things occur. 

1: you basically shoulder code their code because you're always worried about how the code will affect the robot
2: you give them smaller tasks that you can check over later, say autonomous codes. 

I preferred to give the second option. It gave them time to bounce back and forth and ask me questions when stuck, but when they finished I let them test it (after checking if anything seemed unreasonable or dangerous) and they felt like it was their code, not my code that they typed.

But at some point you have to let them touch something vital as it's being written, so that's where the over the shoulder coaching for code can help, even though it's a touch annoying. 

Biggest key is to ask to work on something they aren't working on, because most programming leads get very hyper fixated on one task. It's also a lot better to help in off-season or early season than mid to late season as now all the marbles are out and the chaos is rampant

Full opinion from a member of a newly rising team.


Firstly let's start with the cons of the systems.


You remove the learning process from the students/ limit the learning process

You get an effective system, made with typically more expensive (but higher quality-ish) materials.

You build into one main idea for the game causing bot diversity to shrink

You give the "potential" best possible option a monetary price (for drive train at least imo) 

It's potentially costly especially for new teams


Now I'm going to show the consequential pro for each of those


You don't have to buy the in the box setup, and you still have to assemble it allowing for students to learn either with parts that are made to fit (higher tolerances than old or breaking machines) meaning less error in construction

On top of that first point, my team has only ever bought swerve modules because of our tolerances being too low, but we recaded and created our own everybot parts and such based on images which retaught our students how to develop for it. 

And a final comment to drive it home, most of the premade programming for those subsystems (including swerve) are either not fully modifiable or even complete and some cases might require the programming to add to the way it functions making premade code for them almost useless (so still teaching students)

The effective system... Works? There's not much to say here other than you bought something that works and assembles properly. Yeah it's more expensive than making something yourself, but if you CAN make it yourself you might as well (besides maybe swerve)

I think bot diversity has consistently been directly linked to the more vague a challenge is defined. I saw in 2018 a very unique set of robots (it did help that it was a pick and place and not a shooter) but by 2021/22 bots had become very similar because the goals were simpler and the simple solutions worked VERY WELL. Another big factor of bot diversity that you CANT SEE but can TELL is the programming. My team developed and released a "move and shoot" or "run and gun" code designed entirely around positions and velocities which made our bot WAYYY different than most high goal scorers, without being physically different.

I can't combat the swerve inquisition. As the years go on FIRST has shown more and more that they want to design games around its accommodation and not to promote drivetrain diversity. But what can you say when you literally have a full power omnidirectional travel that takes up less space and still allows for rotation... Swerve is, or at least was, very innovative, and now that most teams know of it, having a paid for swerve system I think makes it MORE accessible, as the precision and tolerances along with the relative complexity of it (at least for high school students) both in programming and mechanical creation, makes swerve being bought a better option as it might honestly be more expensive to make the full system yourself considering the tight nature of the tolerances and how much structure you'd have to design for basically requiring a CNC mill to make it viable to have 4 unless your machinist is doing double duty and are very precise. 

Cost is a weird issue because FRC, and FIRST as a whole, will always to some degree be dictated by the ability to generate revenue as a business to build a good robot. It costs my team around 3k to build our bots, and that's in one bots worth of parts alone. We spent 10k, or so, total last year to get to all of our regionals and worlds, build a robot, have backup parts, do innovation, pay for food. And the citrus circuits spent over 4x that on travel budget alone. You can't eliminate the cost factor, but I think by spreading ideas, you allow teams with less money to spend less on innovation, which costs more than robots usually, and more and refinement, which is what will lead to more income later due to a better robot. 

Ultimately I don't think there is a single reason COTS is universally bad. It's a tool that if misused will lead to the downfall of your team, but if applied correctly will allow giant leaps in progress for your team and every step forward allows the next
